claims.source: When the BL21 bacteria were transformed by PACRG/DNALI1/pCDFDuet-1 plasmid so that both PACRG and DNALI1 were expressed, the PACRG was easily detectable with the Pico system (Figure 2B), indicating that wild-type DNALI1 also stabilizes PACRG protein in bacteria.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from bacterial expression experiments.

claims.claim: DNALI1 is co-purified with His-tagged PACRG when co-expressed in BL21 bacteria.
claims.source: In line with the above interaction data, DNALI1 protein was co-purified with the His-tagged PACRG protein in the same fractions (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by nickel affinity chromatography and western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: DNALI1 and PACRG co-immunoprecipitate from mouse testis extracts.
claims.source: Using anti-PACRG antibody, we searched for the presence of DNALI1 protein in the precipitated complex by performing western blot using specific antibody against DNALI1. The results showed that anti-PACRG antibody specifically pulled down DNALI1 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from mouse testis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: DNALI1 co-localizes with α-tubulin in elongating spermatids.
claims.source: In elongating spermatids, DNALI1 co-localized with the α-tubulin, a manchette marker.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing co-localization.

claims.claim: DNALI1 and PACRG co-localize in elongating spermatids.
claims.source: Double staining with an anti-DNALI1 polyclonal antibody and an anti-PACRG monoclonal antibody revealed that the two proteins also co-localized (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: DNALI1 localization in the manchette is not dependent on PACRG.
claims.source: In Pacrg mutant mice, DNALI1 was still present in the manchette, indicating that the localization of DNALI1 in the manchette is not dependent on PACRG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from Pacrg mutant mice.

claims.claim: Dnali1 cKO mice were generated using a COIN strategy.
claims.source: To explore the role of DNALI1 in vivo, three ES cell clones with conditional potential were previously purchased from HelmholtzZentrum munchen (ES cell clone number: EPD0750_5_E03, order number: MAE-4178) to be injected into blastocysts in order to generate Dnali1 cKO mice. Although chimeric mice were obtained, germline transmission was not successful as evaluated by genotyping at least 200 pups. As a result, we used the COIN strategy to generate Dnali1 cKO mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the mouse generation strategy.

claims.claim: DNALI1 protein is almost absent in Dnali1 cKO mice testes.
claims.source: Subsequent examination of total testicular DNALI1 protein expression by western blot revealed that DNALI1 was almost absent in the cKO mice (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data showing loss of DNALI1 protein.

claims.claim: Dnali1 cKO mice have normal body weight and testis weight.
claims.source: Homozygous Dnali1 cKO mice did not show any gross abnormalities, and their body weight and testis weight were comparable with control mice (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: All homozygous Dnali1 cKO males are infertile.
claims.source: All the wild-type and heterozygous Dnali1 cKO males were fertile and litter sizes were normal. In contrast, all homozygous Dnali1 cKO males examined were infertile (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by breeding study data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Sperm counts are dramatically reduced in Dnali1 cKO mice.
claims.source: Examination of epididymal sperm number, motility, and morphology from the control and homozygous Dnali1 cKO mice revealed that sperm counts and motility were dramatically reduced in the Dnali1 cKO mice (Figure 5D, E and F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Video 1 and Video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sperm count data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Sperm motility is dramatically reduced in Dnali1 cKO mice.
claims.source: Examination of epididymal sperm number, motility, and morphology from the control and homozygous Dnali1 cKO mice revealed that sperm counts and motility were dramatically reduced in the Dnali1 cKO mice (Figure 5D, E and F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Video 1 and Video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sperm motility data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claims.claim: Multiple sperm abnormalities are observed in Dnali1 cKO mice, including head defects and uneven thickness of tails.
claims.source: Multiple sperm abnormalities were observed in the mutant mice, including head defects, uneven thickness of tails, and sperm bundles lacking separation (also called individualization or disengagement) (Figure 6B–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Dnali1 cKO mice exhibit abnormal elongating spermatid heads with compressed shapes in stages I-III.
claims.source: Dnali1 cKO mice exhibited abnormal elongating spermatid heads with compressed shapes and failure to form elongated bundles in stages I-III (Figure 7Ab and c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Dnali1 cKO mice show evidence of spermiation failure.
claims.source: Additionally, normal spermiation was observed in stage VIII-IX seminiferous tubules in the control mice (Figure 7Ag); however, in Dnali1 cKO mice, evidence of spermiation failure was detected by the phagocytosis of thin heads of step 16 spermatids within the epithelium (Figure 7Ah and i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The cauda epididymal lumen in Dnali1 cKO mice contains fewer sperm with abnormal heads and tails and sloughed round spermatids.
claims.source: In Dnali1 cKO mice, the cauda epididymal lumen contained fewer sperm, along with abnormal sperm heads and tails and sloughed round spermatids (Figure 7B, right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Manchette organization appears unaltered in the absence of DNALI1.
claims.source: In the absence of DNALI1, manchette organization appears to be unaltered.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data comparing control and Dnali1 cKO mice shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Dnali1 cKO mice show abnormally condensed chromatin in sperm nuclei.
claims.source: In contrast, in Dnali1 cKO mice, abnormal shapes of the developed sperm nuclei were frequently observed (Figure 9D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 9D.

claims.claim: Dnali1 cKO mice show retained cytoplasmic components in developed sperm.
claims.source: In contrast, in Dnali1 cKO mice, abnormal shapes of the developed sperm nuclei were frequently observed (Figure 9D) and retained cytoplasmic components (not fully resorbed as part of the residual body) were present in the developed sperm (Figure 9E, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: The fibrous sheath shows defective or asymmetric organization in Dnali1 cKO sperm flagella.
claims.source: Importantly, the two longitudinal columns were usually not associated with microtubule doublets 3 and 8, and the two semicircumferential ribs showed defective or asymmetric formations in the principal piece of the flagellum.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data described in the text and shown in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: Some Dnali1 cKO sperm have abnormal cell membranes.
claims.source: Some sperm also had abnormal cell membranes (Figure 9F, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B, C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 9F and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The core '9+2' axoneme is incomplete or disorganized in some Dnali1 cKO sperm.
claims.source: and the core '9+2' axoneme was incomplete or disorganized in some sperm (Figure 9G–I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figures 9G-I.

claims.claim: Testicular protein levels of MEIG1, PACRG, and SPAG16L are unchanged in Dnali1 cKO mice.
claims.source: There was no significant difference in protein levels of MEIG1, PACRG, and SPAG16L between the control and Dnali1 cKO mice (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 10A.

claims.claim: MEIG1 localization in spermatocytes and round spermatids is unchanged in Dnali1 cKO mice.
claims.source: MEIG1 was present in the cell bodies of spermatocytes and round spermatids of control mice, and protein localization was not changed in the two cell types in Dnali1 cKO mice (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: SPAG16L localization in spermatocytes and round spermatids is unchanged in Dnali1 cKO mice.
claims.source: Similarly, SPAG16L was present in the cytoplasm of spermatocytes and round spermatids in both control and Dnali1 cKO mice (Figure 10C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: MEIG1 and SPAG16L do not co-localize in the manchette of elongating spermatids in Dnali1 cKO mice.
claims.source: In contrast, while MEIG1 and SPAG16L were present in elongating spermatids of Dnali1 cKO mice, they appeared not co-localized in the manchette as observed in control mice (Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: The manchette is a transient and unique structure present in elongating spermatids.
claims.source: The manchette is a transient and unique structure present in elongating spermatids and required for proper differentiation of the germ cells during spermatogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claims.claim: The MEIG1/PACRG complex locates in the manchette and is involved in the transport of cargos to build the sperm flagellum.
claims.source: Previous work indicated that the MEIG1/PACRG complex locates in the manchette and is involved in the transport of cargos, such as SPAG16L, to build the sperm flagellum.
claims.evidence: The claim references previous work and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: DNALI1 is an axonemal component originally cloned from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
claims.source: Here, using co-immunoprecipitation and pull-down approaches in various cell systems, we established that DNALI1, an axonemal component originally cloned from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, recruits and stabilizes PACRG
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by literature references.

claims.claim: DNALI1 recruits and stabilizes PACRG.
claims.source: Here, using co-immunoprecipitation and pull-down approaches in various cell systems, we established that DNALI1, an axonemal component originally cloned from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, recruits and stabilizes PACRG
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: DNALI1 is required for the formation of the MEIG1/PACRG complex within the manchette.
claims.source: Importantly, while testicular levels of MEIG1, PACRG, and SPAG16L proteins were unchanged in the Dnali1 mutant mice, their localization within the manchette was greatly affected, indicating that DNALI1 is required for the formation of the MEIG1/PACRG complex within the manchette.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing mislocalization of MEIG1 and SPAG16L in Dnali1 cKO mice.

claims.claim: DNALI1-deficient mice show impaired sperm spermiation/individualization.
claims.source: Interestingly, in contrast to MEIG1 and PACRG-deficient mice, the DNALI1-deficient mice also showed impaired sperm spermiation/individualization, suggesting additional functions beyond its involvement in the manchette structure.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data showing spermiation failure in Dnali1 cKO mice.

claims.claim: Motile cilia have a core '9+2' axonemal structure.
claims.source: Motile cilia are microtubule-based organelles with a core '9+2' axonemal structure (Dutcher, 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Motile cilia dysfunction results in multiple syndromes including male infertility.
claims.source: In humans, motile cilia dysfunction results in multiple syndromes, including bronchiectasis, impaired mucociliary clearance, chronic cough, sinusitis, and male infertility, which are described as immotile cilia syndrome, as well as primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) (Leigh et al., 2009; Noone et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Dynein motor protein complexes are subdivided into inner and outer arms of axonemal ultrastructure.
claims.source: Ciliary beat is driven by dynein motor protein complexes, which are subdivided into the inner and outer arms of axonemal ultrastructure.
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge about ciliary structure.

claims.claim: Loss of dynein function in mammals leads to PCD with ciliary impairment, hydrocephalus, body axis asymmetry, and male infertility.
claims.source: Hence, in mammals the loss of dynein function leads to PCD with ciliary impairment with hydrocephalus, body axis asymmetry, and male infertility (Ibañez-Tallon et al., 2002; Neesen et al., 2001; Supp et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Human DNALI1 gene is the homolog of the Chlamydomonas inner dynein arm gene p28.
claims.source: Human axonemal dynein light intermediate polypeptide 1 (DNALI1) gene is the homolog of the Chlamydomonas inner dynein arm (IDA) gene p28, an important component of the ciliated dynein arm, which is mainly responsible for cilium movement (LeDizet and Piperno, 1995; Kastury et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous molecular characterization studies.

claims.claim: The human DNALI1 gene is localized on chromosome 1 region p35.1.
claims.source: The gene was localized on chromosome 1 region p35.1, and DNALI1 transcripts were detected in several ciliary structures, including sperm flagella, suggesting that this gene could be a good target for patients suffering from immotile cilia syndrome (Kastury et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous molecular analysis.

claims.claim: DNALI1 transcripts are detected in several ciliary structures, including sperm flagella.
claims.source: The gene was localized on chromosome 1 region p35.1, and DNALI1 transcripts were detected in several ciliary structures, including sperm flagella, suggesting that this gene could be a good target for patients suffering from immotile cilia syndrome (Kastury et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous molecular analysis.

claims.claim: DNALI1 has been related to various diseases including frontotemporal lobar degeneration and breast carcinoma.
claims.source: In addition to PCD, DNALI1 was also related to a variety of diseases, including frontotemporal lobar degeneration, diploid breast carcinoma, osteosarcoma, allergic rhinitis, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and Alzheimer's disease (Mishra et al., 2007; Loges et al., 2009; Parris et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2019; Piras et al., 2019), although the precise mechanisms are unclear.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Dnali1 was identified as a sex-related gene involved in spermatogenesis of several fish species.
claims.source: Recently, Dnali1 was identified as a sex-related gene involved in spermatogenesis of several fishes, including the Odontobutis potamophila, the Ussuri catfish Pseudobagrus ussuriensis, and the olive flounder Paralichthys olivaceus (Wang et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent fish studies.

claims.claim: The murine Dnali1 gene is localized on chromosome 4 and consists of six exons.
claims.source: The murine Dnali1 gene is localized on chromosome 4 and consists of six exons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous molecular characterization.

claims.claim: Murine Dnali1 is expressed most strongly in testis.
claims.source: It has two transcripts and is expressed in several tissues but the strongest expression was observed in testis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous expression studies.

claims.claim: During the first wave of spermatogenesis, both Dnali1 mRNA and protein are dramatically increased during spermiogenesis.
claims.source: During the first wave of spermatogenesis, both Dnali1 mRNA and protein were dramatically increased during the spermiogenesis phase, which corresponds to spermatid cell differentiation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous expression studies.

claims.claim: DNALI1 protein is localized in the flagella of mature sperm cells.
claims.source: Moreover, the DNALI1 protein was localized in the flagella of mature sperm cells (Rashid et al., 2006), indicating that Dnali1 may play an essential role in murine sperm formation and male fertility.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous localization studies.

claims.claim: Sperm production consists of mitosis, meiosis, and spermiogenesis.
claims.source: Sperm production and formation is a complex process consisting of mitosis, meiosis, and finally spermiogenesis (Hecht, 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: MEIG1 and PACRG form a protein complex in the manchette.
claims.source: We previously discovered that mouse meiosis-expressed gene 1 (MEIG1) and Parkin co-regulated gene (PACRG) form a protein complex in the manchette, a transient microtubule structure localized in the head compartment of sperm cells during differentiation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The MEIG1/PACRG complex controls sperm flagellum formation, with PACRG being an upstream molecule of MEIG1.
claims.source: It was demonstrated that this protein complex controls sperm flagellum formation, with PACRG being an upstream molecule of MEIG1 (Zhang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Li et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The MEIG1/PACRG complex functions as part of the intramanchette transport system.
claims.source: The MEIG1/PACRG complex was shown to function as part of the cargo transport system, called intramanchette transport (IMT) system (Kierszenbaum, 2002), which transports sperm flagellar proteins, including SPAG16, along the microtubule or F-actin-based transport system to the basal bodies, the template of cilia (Marshall, 2008), for sperm tail assembly.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Intraflagellar transport is a bidirectional process.
claims.source: IFT is a bidirectional process. Through antegrade transport, the cargo proteins are transported from the basal bodies to the tips of cilia/flagella and by the retrograde transport it is possible for the turn-over products to be transported back to the cell body for recycling (Rosenbaum and Witman, 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: MEIG1 was the major binding partner identified in the yeast two-hybrid screen using PACRG as bait.
claims.source: The sequencing results of positive clones revealed that MEIG1 was the major binding partner as previously described (Zhang et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid screening data and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: DNALI1 encoding clones were identified multiple times in the yeast two-hybrid screen.
claims.source: In addition, DNALI1 encoding clones were identified multiple times (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid screening data shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: PACRG/GFP is present in the cytoplasm when expressed alone in CHO cells.
claims.source: When the CHO cells expressed PACRG/GFP only, the protein was present in the cytoplasm (Figure 1Ba)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: DNALI1/FLAG is located on one side of the nucleus as a large granule when expressed alone in CHO cells.
claims.source: while DNALI1/FLAG was located on one side of the nucleus as a large granule (Figure 1Bb).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: PACRG alone is not stable in transfected COS-1 cells with very low protein amount detected.
claims.source: PACRG alone was not stable in the transfected COS-1 cells with very low protein amount detected (Li et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: PACRG was not detectable by the Pico system when bacteria were transformed with PACRG/pCDFDuet-1 plasmid alone.
claims.source: In BL21 bacteria, no PACRG protein was detectable when the less sensitive Pico system was used for western blot analysis after the bacteria were transformed with PACRG/pCDFDuet-1 plasmid and induced by IPTG.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data described in the text.

claims.claim: PACRG was detectable with the Femto system when bacteria were transformed with PACRG/pCDFDuet-1 plasmid alone.
claims.source: However, the PACRG protein was expressed as it was detectable when the higher sensitivity Femto system was used for western blot analysis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data described in the text.

claims.claim: DNALI1 seems to be closer to the nuclear membrane than PACRG in elongating spermatids.
claims.source: DNALI1 seems to be closer to the nuclear membrane, and PACRG is on the surface of DNALI1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observation from immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Germline transmission was not successful when attempting to generate Dnali1 cKO mice from ES cell clones.
claims.source: To explore the role of DNALI1 in vivo, three ES cell clones with conditional potential were previously purchased from HelmholtzZentrum munchen (ES cell clone number: EPD0750_5_E03, order number: MAE-4178) to be injected into blastocysts in order to generate Dnali1 cKO mice. Although chimeric mice were obtained, germline transmission was not successful as evaluated by genotyping at least 200 pups.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the mouse generation attempts.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas9 was used to insert a COIN cassette in intron 1 of Dnali1.
claims.source: To this end, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to insert a COIN cassette in intron 1 of Dnali1 to generate the cKO mouse line (see supplemental for details) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and shown in supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Dnali1COIN/COIN mice were crossed with Stra8-iCre mice to obtain Dnali1 cKO mice.
claims.source: Dnali1COIN/COIN mice were crossed with Stra8-iCre mice to obtain Dnali1COIN/COIN; Stra8-iCre+/- mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b; hereafter Dnali1 cKO) with Dnali1 gene specifically disrupted in male germ cells (Dnali1 cKO).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the breeding strategy.

claims.claim: Sperm from control mice show normal morphology.
claims.source: Sperm from the control mice showed normal morphology (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Control testis seminiferous tubule epithelium shows elongated spermatid heads embedded as bundles among round spermatids in stages I-III.
claims.source: In control mice, the seminiferous tubule epithelium showed elongated spermatid heads embedded as bundles among the round spermatids, with developing tails extending into the lumen in stages I-III (Figure 7Aa).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Control stage XII seminiferous tubules show step 12 elongating spermatid bundles with large pachytene spermatocytes in meiotic division.
claims.source: In stage XII, the control seminiferous tubule epithelium showed step 12 elongating spermatid bundles with large pachytene spermatocytes in meiotic division (Figure 7Ad).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Dnali1 cKO mice show abnormal elongating spermatid heads without normal bundle formation in stage XII.
claims.source: However, in Dnali1 cKO mice, stage XII showed abnormal elongating spermatid heads without normal bundle formation (Figure 7Ae and f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Control mice show normal spermiation in stage VIII-IX seminiferous tubules.
claims.source: Additionally, normal spermiation was observed in stage VIII-IX seminiferous tubules in the control mice (Figure 7Ag)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Control cauda epididymis shows the lumen filled with normal sperm heads and tails.
claims.source: The control cauda epididymis shows the lumen filled with normal sperm heads (H) and tails (T).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Numerous mature sperm are concentrated in the cauda epididymis of control mice.
claims.source: Numerous mature sperm were concentrated in the cauda epididymis of control mice (Figure 7B, left).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Control mice show nuclei with normally condensed chromatin in testis seminiferous tubule epithelium.
claims.source: In control mice, the developed sperm nuclei had normal elongated shapes with condensed chromatin (Figure 9A)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Control mice show normal midpiece of flagella with normal '9+2' axoneme structure surrounded by mitochondrial sheath and ODF.
claims.source: and the flagella contain a normal '9+2' axoneme structure surrounded by accessory structures, including the mitochondrial sheath (Figure 9B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: Control mice show normal principal piece of flagella with complete fibrous sheath.
claims.source: and a fibrous sheath (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: In control mice, the two longitudinal columns of the fibrous sheath are associated with microtubule doublets 3 and 8.
claims.source: The fibrous sheath consists of two longitudinal columns (LC) connected by semicircumferential ribs (R). The two longitudinal columns are associated with microtubule doublets 3 and 8, and the two semicircumferential ribs are symmetrical.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data and description of control mice in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: The fibrous sheath is a cytoskeletal structure of the principal piece in the flagellum.
claims.source: The fibrous sheath is a cytoskeletal structure of the principal piece in the flagellum, which consists of two longitudinal columns connected by semicircular ribs.
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge about sperm structure.

claims.claim: The longitudinal columns of the fibrous sheath are attached to outer dense fibers 3 and 8 in the anterior part of the principal piece.
claims.source: The longitudinal columns are attached to outer dense fibers 3 and 8 in the anterior part of the principal piece and replace those fibers in the middle and posterior part of the principal piece and become associated with microtubule doublets 3 and 8 (Fawcett, 1975).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Spermiation/individualization is one of the final steps of spermiogenesis.
claims.source: Spermiation/individualization is one of the final steps of spermiogenesis and the defects are a common cause of human male infertility (Cooper, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Defects in spermiation/individualization are a common cause of human male infertility.
claims.source: Spermiation/individualization is one of the final steps of spermiogenesis and the defects are a common cause of human male infertility (Cooper, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: In Drosophila, sperm individualization occurs when the individualized complex is assembled around the nucleus of each bundle of 64 haploid elongated spermatid nuclei.
claims.source: In Drosophila, this occurs when the membrane cytoskeleton individualized complex (IC) is assembled around the nucleus of each bundle of 64 haploid elongated spermatid nuclei.
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge about Drosophila spermatogenesis.

claims.claim: In mammals, spermiation is thought to be driven by tubulobulbar complexes.
claims.source: In mammals, the process is thought to be driven by tubulobulbar complexes (TBC) and involves the removal of ectoplasmic specializations, and actin filament networks are also the major components of TBCs (Hess and Vogl, 2015; Cooper, 2005; O'Donnell et al., 2011; Tokuyasu et al., 1972; Adams et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: At least 70 genes are involved in the process of spermiation/individualization.
claims.source: It has been reported using genetic studies that at least 70 genes are involved in the process of spermiation/individualization, with a unique cooperation between Sertoli cells and the maturing elongated spermatids (Hess and Vogl, 2015; Steinhauer, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claims.claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton is important for spermiation/individualization.
claims.source: The microtubule cytoskeleton is important for spermiation/individualization (Steinhauer, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Mutations in components of the dynein-dynein complex disrupt the synchronous movement of actin cones.
claims.source: Mutations in the components of the dynein-dynein complex, including the cytoplasmic dynein intermediate chain, the two Drosophila dynein light chains DDLC1 and DLC90F, disrupt the synchronous movement of actin cones, but they also disrupt the nucleus shaping and positioning (Ghosh-Roy et al., 2005; Ghosh-Roy et al., 2004; Li et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: DNALI1 is present along the entire length of the sperm flagellar axoneme.
claims.source: This would not be surprising in sperm, as it is present along the entire length of the sperm flagellar axoneme (Rashid et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous localization studies.

claims.claim: Dynein proteins are present in the outer dynein arms and inner dynein arms of the axonemal complex.
claims.source: Dynein proteins are present in the outer dynein arms (ODAs) and IDAs of the axonemal complex, and both arms are essential for the beating of cilia and flagella (Kamiya and Okamoto, 1985; Mitchell and Rosenbaum, 1985).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Inner dynein arms have seven major subspecies and four minor subspecies.
claims.source: IDAs have seven major subspecies and four minor subspecies (Scholey, 2008), but little is known about the functional differences between these subspecies (Bui et al., 2012; Yagi et al., 2005; Kamiya and Yagi, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: CHO cells were cultured with DMEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum at 37°C.
claims.source: The CHO cells were cultured with DMEM (with 10% fetal bovine serum) at 37°C.
claims.evidence: The claim is a methodological detail stated in the Materials and methods section.

results.result: DNALI1 physically interacts with PACRG in multiple experimental systems. The interaction was demonstrated through yeast two-hybrid screening, co-immunoprecipitation in mammalian cells and mouse testis, co-localization in CHO cells and elongating spermatids, luciferase complementation assay, and co-purification from bacteria. DNALI1 does not interact with MEIG1.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent experimental approaches (C1-C6, C10-C11, C13, C60) consistently demonstrate DNALI1-PACRG interaction across different systems (yeast, bacteria, mammalian cells, mouse testis). The negative control showing no DNALI1-MEIG1 interaction (C5) strengthens specificity. The convergence of evidence from diverse methodologies provides robust support.

results.result: DNALI1 stabilizes PACRG protein post-translationally in both mammalian cells and bacteria. Co-expression of DNALI1 dramatically increases PACRG protein levels without affecting Pacrg mRNA levels, indicating a post-transcriptional stabilization mechanism.
results.evaluation: The stabilization effect is demonstrated in multiple systems (COS-1 cells: C7-C8; bacteria: C9, C64-C65) with appropriate controls showing PACRG instability alone (C63-C65). The qPCR data (C8) rules out transcriptional effects, supporting post-translational stabilization. The consistency across systems strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: DNALI1 co-localizes with PACRG and α-tubulin in the manchette of elongating spermatids, and DNALI1 localization is independent of PACRG. This suggests DNALI1 is an upstream component of the MEIG1/PACRG complex.
results.evaluation: Immunofluorescence data (C12-C13) demonstrate co-localization in wild-type mice. The persistence of DNALI1 in the manchette of Pacrg mutant mice (C14) establishes independence and upstream positioning (C112). The spatial relationship observation (C66) provides additional structural context. The logic is sound and data are consistent.

results.result: Dnali1 conditional knockout mice were successfully generated using COIN strategy after failed ES cell approach. The Dnali1COIN/COIN mice crossed with Stra8-iCre resulted in male germ cell-specific knockout with near-complete loss of DNALI1 protein in testes.
results.evaluation: The mouse generation strategy is clearly documented (C15, C67-C69, C102-C103) with appropriate validation showing DNALI1 protein depletion (C16). The use of Stra8-iCre for germ cell-specific knockout is well-established (C103). The methodological details are sufficient for reproducibility.

results.result: Dnali1 cKO male mice exhibit complete infertility with dramatically reduced sperm count and motility, despite normal body and testis weights. All homozygous mutant males failed to produce offspring after 2 months of breeding.
results.evaluation: The fertility assessment (C18, C104) and sperm parameters (C19-C20) are quantified with appropriate controls. Normal gross phenotype (C17) indicates specific reproductive defects. The breeding duration (C104) is adequate for fertility assessment. Statistical significance is indicated for sperm parameters.

results.result: Dnali1 cKO mice produce sperm with multiple morphological abnormalities including head defects, uneven tail thickness, and failure of sperm individualization, contrasting with normal sperm morphology in controls.
results.evaluation: Microscopy data (C21, C70) document specific morphological defects with visual evidence. The range of abnormalities (head, tail, individualization) suggests pleiotropic effects. Control comparison (C70) establishes baseline normal morphology. The observations are consistent with the infertility phenotype.

results.result: Histological analysis reveals impaired spermiogenesis in Dnali1 cKO mice with abnormal spermatid head morphology, failure of bundle formation, spermiation defects, and reduced sperm in the epididymis compared to controls showing normal spermatogenesis.
results.evaluation: Detailed stage-specific histological analysis (C22-C24, C71-C76) documents progressive defects throughout spermiogenesis. Control comparisons at each stage establish normal baseline. The spermiation failure (C23) is a novel phenotype not seen in MEIG1/PACRG mutants. The histological evidence is comprehensive and well-documented.

results.result: Manchette organization appears morphologically normal in Dnali1 cKO mice based on α-tubulin staining patterns.
results.evaluation: Immunofluorescence comparison (C25) shows similar α-tubulin distribution between control and mutant. This distinguishes DNALI1 function from manchette assembly per se, suggesting a role in cargo transport rather than structural organization. However, more detailed ultrastructural analysis might reveal subtle defects.

results.result: Transmission electron microscopy reveals multiple ultrastructural defects in Dnali1 cKO sperm including abnormal nuclear chromatin condensation, retained cytoplasm, disorganized fibrous sheath, abnormal membranes, and incomplete/disorganized axonemes, contrasting with normal ultrastructure in controls.
results.evaluation: TEM analysis (C26-C30, C77-C80) provides detailed ultrastructural evidence of defects at multiple levels. Control images establish normal baseline structure. The fibrous sheath defects (C28) are particularly notable with specific misalignment of longitudinal columns. The range of defects supports pleiotropic roles for DNALI1.

results.result: While testicular protein levels of MEIG1, PACRG, and SPAG16L remain unchanged in Dnali1 cKO mice, these proteins fail to properly localize to the manchette in elongating spermatids, indicating DNALI1 is required for MEIG1/PACRG complex formation within the manchette.
results.evaluation: Western blot data (C31) establish unchanged total protein levels, while immunofluorescence (C32-C34) demonstrates mislocalization specifically in elongating spermatids. This dissociation between expression and localization strongly supports DNALI1's role in complex assembly/localization (C39). The cell-type specific analysis strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Dnali1 cKO mice show impaired spermiation/individualization not observed in MEIG1/PACRG-deficient mice, suggesting additional DNALI1 functions. This may involve dysregulation of autophagy and interaction with γ-actin.
results.evaluation: The spermiation defect (C40) is well-documented, but the mechanistic links to autophagy (C111) and γ-actin (C122) are speculative. The autophagy marker upregulation is shown but causality is not established. The γ-actin interaction is from a separate screen without validation in the current study. Additional experiments are needed to confirm these mechanisms.

results.result: ATG16L and ATG5 autophagy markers are significantly upregulated in Dnali1 cKO testes, suggesting potential dysregulation of autophagy.
results.evaluation: Western blot data (C110) with statistical analysis demonstrate significant upregulation of both autophagy markers. However, this is correlative evidence; whether autophagy dysregulation is causal for the phenotype or a secondary consequence remains unclear. The connection to spermiation failure (C111) is inferential.

results.result: DNALI1 likely associates with manchette microtubules through dynein heavy chain 1 (DYNC1H1) and serves as the major driving force for transporting the MEIG1/PACRG complex along manchette microtubules.
results.evaluation: The presence of DYNC1H1 in the manchette is shown, and the reported DNALI1-DYNC1H1 interaction is cited (C113). However, direct demonstration of this interaction in the manchette context is lacking. The motor function claim (C114) is highly plausible given DNALI1's identity as a dynein component, but direct evidence of motor activity or transport is not provided.

results.result: The abnormal sperm phenotype in Dnali1 cKO mice appears to result from disruption of both IMT and IFT pathways. Basal body formation appears normal, but DNALI1 may be involved in IFT based on its presence in developing flagella and observed ultrastructural defects.
results.evaluation: The dual pathway disruption hypothesis (C116) is reasonable given the phenotypic complexity, and normal basal bodies (C117) rule out one alternative explanation. However, the IFT involvement (C118, C121) is largely inferential based on DNALI1 localization and morphological defects. Direct functional evidence for IFT disruption (e.g., IFT particle tracking, cargo accumulation studies) is lacking.

results.result: DNALI1 has multiple roles in sperm formation and function, with a clearly demonstrated main function in IMT associated with the MEIG1/PACRG complex, and potential additional roles in IFT and sperm individualization that require further investigation.
results.evaluation: The IMT function (C124, C127) is well-supported by the localization and genetic interaction data. The acknowledgment that additional roles (C125, C128) require further investigation is appropriately cautious. The summary (C123, C126) accurately reflects the strength and limitations of the evidence. This represents a balanced conclusion.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on manchette structure and function, MEIG1/PACRG complex, DNALI1 evolutionary conservation and expression, ciliary structure, sperm development, and spermiation/individualization processes, establishing the biological context for the study.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout. They provide necessary context for interpreting the experimental results. The citations appear appropriate and the background information is accurately represented. This is standard practice for scientific manuscripts.

results.result: The manuscript provides detailed methodological information for cell culture, transfection, microscopy, co-immunoprecipitation, bacterial expression, luciferase assays, western blotting, mouse breeding, sperm analysis, histology, and electron microscopy, with appropriate reagents, equipment, and statistical methods specified.
results.evaluation: The methods are described in sufficient detail for reproducibility (C93-C109). Specific reagents, equipment models, and protocols are provided. The statistical approach (C109) is appropriate for the data types. These methodological details support the validity of the experimental results and enable replication.
